Canada's top court has upheld Quebec's controversial secular law.
As done, Carpentruck reports the law prevents public sector workers from wearing religious symbols while on the job.
Quebec's Bill 21 came into law in 2019, a bid to separate religion and state.
It meant that certain public sector employees such as judges, police officers and teachers were prevented from wearing religious symbols.
The Chief Justice of Canada's Supreme Court stated that the law is rooted in a legitimate and historical commitment to ensure the separation of religion and state in a democratic society.
The impacts were felt by Muslim women who wore hijabs, Sikhs who wore turbans and Jews who wore kippas.
The only part of the law the court agreed was unconstitutional was that it prevented elected members of the Quebec National Assembly from wearing face coverings.
For NPR News, I'm Dan Carpentruck in Toronto.

Retailers are counting on Black Friday to be the busiest shopping day of the year.
NPR's Alina Seljuk reports holiday spending is expected to set a record this season.
The National Retail Federation estimates that almost 183 million people will be shopping this long Thanksgiving weekend.
This number is actually a bit lower from last year, but the overall holiday spending is expected to keep rising from last year.

In Puerto Rico, thousands gathered in front of the largest mall in the Caribbean on Black Friday, not to shop, but to protest ongoing blackouts, high electricity rates and the high cost of living there.
This comes just days after the Island Supreme Court ruled in favor of the governor to fire the private company Luma Energy.
That's the operator that has been managing the power grid for the last five years.
But the court also gave Luma 10 days to appeal the ruling.
The company said in a statement that this matter goes beyond a contractual dispute with significant implications on Puerto Rico's energy future.
